subject: Art & Design
title: Design Systems: Scaling Consistency
description: A fast breakdown of Design Systems: Scaling Consistency for builders.

hook.text: Google has 1,000+ products. Without Material Design, each one would look like a different company.

buildup.text: A design system is a library of reusable components, patterns, and guidelines that enforce consistency.

discovery.text: It includes tokens (colors, spacing), components (buttons, cards), and documentation (when to use what).

twist.text: Design systems don't limit creativity — they free designers from reinventing basic elements every time.

climax.text: Airbnb, IBM, Shopify, and Atlassian all publish their design systems publicly. It's an industry norm.

punchline.text: A system isn't a style guide. It's a living product that serves products.

quiz.question: What does a design system contain?
options: Tokens, reusable components, and usage documentation

details.summary: Design systems are documented collections of reusable components — buttons, colors, typography, spacing, icons — that ensure visual consistency across products and teams.
details.whyItMatters: Without design systems, large organizations produce inconsistent, confusing products. Design systems solve the problem of scaling quality by turning design decisions into shared, reusable building blocks.
takeaways: Design systems document reusable components for consistency
Material Design and Apple HIG are prominent examples
Systems enable large teams to create cohesive experiences

faq.question: What's the difference between a style guide and a design system?
faq.answer: A style guide documents visual rules (colors, fonts, logo usage). A design system goes further, providing coded reusable components (buttons, forms, cards), usage guidelines, accessibility standards, and design tokens. It's both documentation and a living toolkit that designers and developers share.

faq.question: How big does a company need to be to need a design system?
faq.answer: Any team with more than one designer or developer benefits from documenting shared components. Formal design systems become essential when multiple teams build different parts of a product. The investment pays off when consistency problems start costing more than building the system.
